The "systems of record" line is the real shift. In customer engagement, the conversation happens on WhatsApp and Instagram, but the record lives in the CRM or ticketing tool. Agents that only sit on top inherit that gap. The ones that write back to the record, with state and an audit trail, close it. Curious how governance keeps up when the factory ships apps faster than IT can review them.

More agents make systems of record more important, not less, and nowhere more than in ERP. Today one supplier delay can mean 350 switches across 22 systems, with people acting as the middleware. Headless ERP (like Dynamics 365 ERP) plus Copilot’s context lets agents connect transactional truth with business intent. But as with the PC, the payoff comes from redesigning the work, not just adding to it. The factory builds the software; partners bring the judgment on what to build.

Satya, I think the harder transition is not making SaaS “infinite,” but making system of record changes safe enough to be executed by agents at scale. Once Copilot moves from retrieving context to orchestrating actions across ERP, CRM, finance, supply chain and other systems, the critical control point becomes the state transition itself: what can an agent change, under which invariants, with what authority, and how is the resulting state independently verified? That may be the real definition of “governed” in an infinite SaaS factory. How is Microsoft thinking about that execution boundary?

[Satya Nadella](https://www.linkedin.com/in/satyanadella?trk=public_post_comment-text) , as a security guy, I worry that an infinite SaaS factory also means an infinite attack surface. What happens when a supplier sends an invoice with a hidden prompt injection, and a user-built app with ERP write access reads it? The app changes the bank details and the payment goes out. No phishing click, no stolen password. Every app this factory builds is a new privileged identity. Let’s make sure each one gets least privilege by default.

Sometimes the problem is not how fast technology evolves, but how quickly the direction keeps changing. Microsoft is a clear example: Copilot → AI coding → agents → agentic applications → Copilot as a new layer for work →... Every few months, engineers hear a new version of “this is the future.” For ambitious people trying to keep up, this constant change can be exhausting. Maybe we should focus less on chasing every wave and more on skills that survive the waves.


[Shekhar Dhongade](https://www.linkedin.com/in/shekhardhongade?trk=public_post_comment_actor-name) 4w


The vision of Copilot evolving into a unified System of Interaction and orchestration layer is a compelling shift.Historically, the explosion of SaaS provided specialized Systems of Record across functions, but forced end users to constantly context-switch across fragmented interfaces, disparate UX models, and siloed workflows. Unifying interaction and governance through an agentic layer directly addresses that friction. It raises an intriguing question for the future of business applications: As natural language and AI agents become the primary UI for executing work, are traditional SaaS UX/UI design investments becoming obsolete—or simply shifting focus entirely from human interaction design to API and agent-orchestration readiness? Would love to hear how leaders see the role of traditional application UX evolving in an agentic-first world.
